title: The Next Phase of China’s Minority Crackdown
gist: China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, effective July 1, 2026, converts a decade of de facto assimilation policy into binding national legislation — mandating Mandarin in education and official life, requiring shared Chinese cultural symbols in public space, and directing officials to use AI to standardize the national image. Leibold and Dorjee argue this hollows out constitutional territorial autonomy without repealing it, embeds the policy in bureaucratic structures that would survive Xi, and destroys the autonomy middle ground once occupied by the Dalai Lama and Ilham Tohti — pushing exile movements toward independence demands and locking Beijing into permanent coercion.

themes.theme: Ethnic Unity Law Codifies Forced Assimilation

insights.claim: As of July 1, 2026, China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress makes national integration through forced cultural assimilation the law of the land, passed by the full National People's Congress rather than imposed by administrative fiat.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
entities: Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress
insights.so_what: NPC-level enactment signals Beijing treats ethnic homogenization as a core state interest, raising the ceiling on Western human-rights sanctions and supply-chain scrutiny risk for firms sourcing from Xinjiang and Tibet.
insights.locator: As of July 1, however, national integration

insights.claim: Xi did not repeal China's existing autonomy framework — which formally remains in place alongside a constitution still defining China as a multinational state — but imposed a parallel statutory framework that empties autonomy of substantive meaning.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Legal-layering rather than repeal is the governance technique to watch across Chinese policy: formal guarantees survive as facade while new statutes control actual practice.
insights.locator: He did not repeal the existing framework

insights.claim: The new law makes Mandarin the basic language of education and official life nationwide and requires museums, heritage sites, public buildings, and place names to display shared Chinese cultural symbols.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: A nationwide mandate over signage, naming, and curricula creates real compliance cost and physical rebranding demand across minority regions.
insights.locator: The new ethnic unity law makes Mandarin Chinese

insights.claim: The law requires Chinese state officials to use new technologies, including artificial intelligence, to promote a standardized image of the Chinese nation.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: A statutory AI mandate for cultural standardization creates a domestic procurement channel for Chinese AI and content-generation vendors tied to state ideology work.
insights.locator: and requires state officials to use new technologies

insights.claim: The law extends to family life, directing parents and guardians of minority children to educate them to love the party, the motherland, and the Chinese nation, and exposes individuals and organizations outside China to administrative penalties, detention, or criminal prosecution for creating ethnic division.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Extraterritorial reach means diaspora organizations, foreign NGOs, and researchers face legal exposure — a compliance and travel-risk factor for any entity engaging Chinese minority issues.
insights.locator: Even family life is drawn into the project

insights.claim: Because the campaign is now embedded in bureaucratic practice and institutional structure, even a more liberal successor to Xi would need a complete bureaucratic, political, and cultural overhaul to revive minority autonomy.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Institutionalization makes this policy persistence-proof against leadership change — do not price a post-Xi liberalization scenario on ethnic policy.
insights.quote: Beijing has closed the door on peaceful coexistence.

themes.theme: Soviet Collapse and Second-Generation Ethnic Policy

insights.claim: The People's Republic was founded in 1949 as an explicitly multinational state whose bargain was that national unity would be best secured by recognizing difference and granting minorities limited territorial, linguistic, and political autonomy rather than forcing absorption into Han culture.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline the 2026 law abandons — the magnitude of the reversal, not the crackdown itself, is what is new.
insights.locator: When the People’s Republic of China was founded

insights.claim: China's Soviet-inspired system recognizes 56 formally equal nationalities and was codified by a 1984 law entitling minority groups in regions from Xinjiang to Yunnan to use their own languages as the medium of school instruction.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Forty years of statutory language rights are being reversed in a single statute, an unusually abrupt legal discontinuity for Chinese governance.
insights.locator: China’s official policy, inspired by the Soviet model

insights.claim: Advocates of a second-generation ethnic policy, emerging after the Soviet collapse, argued that Soviet-inspired territorial autonomy hardened ethnic boundaries and created the conditions for separatism, putting China at risk of disintegrating along nationality-based lines as the USSR did.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: The intellectual driver is fear of Soviet-style disintegration, which means the policy will intensify rather than moderate whenever Beijing perceives centrifugal risk.
insights.locator: Starting around the first decade of the twenty-first century

insights.claim: China's autonomous regions are far more tightly controlled than Soviet federal republics were and possess neither sovereignty nor a legal route to independence, making the Soviet-disintegration analogy that drives Beijing's policy factually weak.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Beijing is solving a threat that does not structurally exist, which means the coercion is likely to overshoot and generate the backlash it fears.
insights.locator: Although the situation in Beijing is fundamentally different

insights.claim: Xi's dismantling of territorial autonomy is commonly traced to the 2008 Lhasa uprising across the Tibetan plateau and the 2009 Urumqi riots in Xinjiang, in which nearly 200 people were killed according to official figures.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: The authors treat the unrest as trigger rather than cause — the policy's real roots predate Xi, so removing unrest would not reverse it.

themes.theme: Politicide: Camps, Boarding Schools, Language Erasure

insights.claim: Mongolian scholar Uradyn Bulag's concept of politicide — the destruction of a people's capacity to understand itself and act as a distinct political community — describes Xi's project of remaking the inner life of China's non-Han peoples so that claims to distinct political identity become hard to imagine, mobilize, or transmit.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: A distinct analytical category from genocide or repression, useful for assessing state strategies that target collective political capacity rather than physical survival.
insights.quote: Xi has sought to remake the inner life of China’s non-Han peoples.

insights.claim: Starting in 2017, Xinjiang authorities detained an estimated one million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in political reeducation camps, and Beijing has placed nearly a million Tibetan children in state-run boarding schools including preschools.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Two roughly million-person coercive programs sustain the forced-labor and import-ban exposure that already governs Xinjiang-linked supply chains in solar, cotton, and electronics.

insights.claim: When Inner Mongolia required key school subjects to be taught in Mandarin in 2020, Mongolian students and parents organized boycotts and demonstrations, and party authorities responded by detaining protesters, punishing teachers, and purging Mongolian officials from party leadership.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the state's escalation pattern — including cadre purges — that will now repeat nationwide under statutory authority.

insights.claim: Language erasure is measurably working, with the nationalist Global Times reporting as early as 2016 that some Tibetan children were losing the ability to converse easily with parents and grandparents, and recent social media videos showing children struggling to pronounce their own names in Tibetan.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Intergenerational language loss is the metric Beijing reads as success, which means the policy has positive feedback and will be extended rather than reversed.
insights.locator: The nationalist newspaper Global Times reported as early as 2016

insights.claim: Xi's signature formulation 'forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation' sounds like benign civic nationalism in English, but the Chinese verb for forging is the same word used for casting molten ore into unbreakable iron, revealing an intent to mold individual consciousness.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: A concrete lesson in translation asymmetry: official Chinese slogans routinely read softer in English than in the original, which systematically biases Western readings of Beijing's intent.
insights.quote: forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation
insights.locator: At its heart is one of Xi’s signature formulations

insights.claim: Political theorist Will Kymlicka's distinction between immigrant communities seeking equal citizenship and colonized national minorities seeking collective continuity on ancestral territory explains why Mongols, Tibetans, and Uyghurs will not accept assimilation traded for equal opportunity.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Explains why economic development offers in minority regions do not buy political acquiescence — the demands are categorically different from immigrant integration.

insights.claim: The Dalai Lama, Han writer Wang Lixiong, and Uyghur economist Ilham Tohti long occupied a shrinking middle ground arguing that meaningful autonomy, not independence, offered a realistic path to interethnic reconciliation — and all three have now been neutralized.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: With moderates removed, no negotiating counterparty remains — any future Tibet or Xinjiang settlement would have to be built from scratch with more radical actors.
insights.locator: For decades, prominent figures such as the Dalai Lama

insights.claim: The party claims exclusive authority to select and recognize the Dalai Lama's successor, Wang Lixiong's work is barred from publication and he has been prevented from leaving China since 2015, and Ilham Tohti is serving a life sentence on separatism charges.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: The succession claim sets up a near-certain Tibetan legitimacy crisis and a diplomatic flashpoint with India and the United States when the current Dalai Lama dies.
insights.locator: By formally hollowing out the autonomy

insights.claim: The law permits ethnic costumes, food, and music only as commercialized spectacle for Han tourists and officials, curated and detached from the communities that produce it, while anything suggesting distinct collective identity or self-rule is barred.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Minority culture becomes a tourism product line rather than a political fact — expect state-backed ethnic tourism investment alongside intensifying repression.
insights.locator: The law does not prohibit diversity

insights.claim: Minority communities will be pushed toward a double life of public conformity and private preservation, with language, religion, and historical memory retreating into homes, informal networks, and diaspora institutions outside mainland China.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Cultural authority migrates offshore, making exile institutions the durable center of gravity and increasing friction between Beijing and host countries that harbor them.
insights.locator: Minority communities that seek to maintain their culture

insights.claim: Coercive integration historically hardens political claims that outlive the state's reach, as when late-Soviet backlash against Russification fueled Baltic reform movements that became independence movements, and Milosevic's 1989 dismantling of Kosovo's autonomy destroyed confidence in Yugoslavia's federal compact.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Two historical precedents where autonomy revocation preceded state disintegration — the tail risk Beijing is creating is precisely the one it means to eliminate.
insights.locator: In the late Soviet Union, for example, backlash against Russification

insights.claim: China's far greater coercive capacity makes Soviet- or Yugoslav-style internal mobilization unlikely for now, but demands for outright independence are likely to grow among Mongolian, Tibetan, and Uyghur activists in exile.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: The near-term instability shows up abroad, not inside China — expect escalating diaspora activism and corresponding Chinese transnational repression, a diplomatic irritant rather than a market event.
insights.locator: China’s far greater coercive capacity

insights.claim: One day after the law took effect, Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen self-immolated outside United Nations headquarters in New York, capturing the polarizing effect of destroying the middle ground between assimilation and separation.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: An early signal of the radicalization channel the authors predict; a rising frequency of such acts would confirm the thesis.
insights.locator: On July 2, one day after China’s new law took effect

insights.claim: By dismantling autonomy, Xi may find that his only remaining option for preserving national unity is a state of permanent coercion.
insights.speaker: James Leibold
insights.so_what: Permanent coercion means a permanently elevated internal security budget and a standing reputational and sanctions overhang on Chinese assets tied to minority regions.
